title: 02. Networking, Protocols & APIs: Reverse Proxy
summary: A reverse proxy is a server-side proxy that intercepts incoming client requests and forwards them to one or more backend servers, then returns the backend's response to the client — providing a single, controlled entry point…
objectives: What is a reverse proxy, and how is it different from a forward proxy?
What load balancing algorithms does a reverse proxy use, and when would you pick each?
How does TLS termination at a reverse proxy work, and what are the trade-offs?
How do health checks work in a reverse proxy, and why do you need both active and passive?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A reverse proxy is a server-side proxy that intercepts incoming client requests and forwards them to one or more backend servers, then returns the backend's response to the client — providing a single, controlled entry point that can perform load balancing, TLS termination, caching, rate limiting, routing, observability, and protocol translation without the client or backend knowing it is there.
A reverse proxy sits in front of your backend servers and acts as the single public face of your application. To the client, the reverse proxy looks like the origin — it has the public IP, terminates TLS, and responds to HTTP requests. To the backend, the reverse proxy looks like just another HTTP client — it opens a connection, sends a request, reads a response. The proxy decouples the client's view of the service (a single hostname like `api.example.com`) from the actual implementation (3 backend instances on private IPs, autoscaling, replacing each other constantly). This decoupling is what makes modern deployment possible: you can deploy a new version of the backend by adding it to the proxy's pool, draining traffic from the old version, and removing the old version — all without changing anything the client sees. NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, AWS ALB, and Google's GFE are all reverse proxies.

The contrast with a forward proxy is the foundational distinction. A forward proxy sits in front of clients (e.g., a corporate web filter, or `squid` at a school); it lets clients reach the internet while hiding the clients' identities and enforcing policy. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers; it lets clients reach your servers while hiding the servers' identities and enforcing policy. The same software can do both — `nginx` and `haproxy` can be configured either way — but the operational role is opposite. The forward proxy is "I am a client, hide me from the server"; the reverse proxy is "I am the server, hide my backends from the client." This distinction matters in interviews because people confuse the two constantly. The way to remember: a forward proxy proxies on behalf of the client (forward = outbound), a reverse proxy proxies on behalf of the server (reverse = inbound).

The first major use case is **load balancing**. A reverse proxy maintains a pool of backend instances and distributes incoming requests across them. Algorithms include round-robin (each backend in turn), least-connections (send to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests, best for variable request cost), IP-hash (consistent hashing on client IP for session affinity), and weighted (give backends different shares based on capacity). Health checks are essential: the proxy polls each backend periodically (e.g., `GET /health` every 5 seconds) and removes unhealthy backends from the pool automatically. AWS ALB, NGINX, and Envoy all support active health checks (polling) and passive health checks (count failures from real traffic and remove after N consecutive 5xx or timeouts). The trade-off: more backends = more fault tolerance but more coordination; fewer backends = simpler but bigger blast radius of failure.

The second major use case is **TLS termination**. The reverse proxy terminates the client's TLS connection (holds the certificate, does the handshake, decrypts incoming records), then forwards plaintext HTTP to the backend over a private network. This offloads CPU-expensive crypto from the backend (significant at thousands of requests per second) and centralizes certificate management — you renew one cert on the proxy, not 50 certs across 50 backend instances. The backend can be plain HTTP (Cloudflare's "Flexible" mode, not recommended) or re-encrypted TLS to the backend ("Full strict" mode, recommended for sensitive data). NGINX and Envoy also support mTLS to the backend, which is the foundation of service meshes — Istio's Envoy sidecars do exactly this, terminating mTLS from the upstream sidecar and re-establishing mTLS to the downstream sidecar.

The third major use case is **caching and static content**. The proxy can cache responses from the backend, returning cached responses for subsequent identical requests without touching the backend at all. NGINX's `proxy_cache_path` directive, Varnish (a purpose-built caching reverse proxy), and Cloudflare's edge cache all do this. The fourth is **rate limiting and authentication** — the proxy can apply rate limits per client IP or per API key, validate JWTs, check OAuth scopes, and reject unauthorized requests before they touch the backend. The fifth is **routing** — path-based routing (`/api/*` to one backend pool, `/static/*` to another, `/admin/*` to a third), host-based routing (`api.example.com` to one pool, `www.example.com` to another), and protocol translation (terminate HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 from the client, forward as HTTP/1.1 to a legacy backend). The sixth is **observability** — the proxy is the single chokepoint where you can log every request, emit metrics (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles), and trace headers.

Real-world deployments are everywhere. **Netflix** runs NGINX at the edge of its API tier, terminating TLS, rate-limiting per device, and routing to Zuul (their Java gateway) which then routes to internal microservices. **AWS ALB** (Application Load Balancer) is a managed reverse proxy that does path-based routing, TLS termination, health-checked load balancing, and integration with ECS/EKS for autoscaling. **Envoy** is the foundation of the Istio and Consul service meshes — it runs as a sidecar container in every pod, intercepting all traffic in and out via iptables, and provides mTLS, traffic splitting, circuit breaking, and rich observability. **Google's GFE** (Google Front End) is the reverse proxy that fronts every Google service (Search, Gmail, YouTube) — it terminates TLS, does global routing, applies security policies, and is the foundation of Google's BeyondCorp zero-trust model. **Cloudflare's edge** is itself a massive reverse proxy network, sitting in front of millions of customer origins.

The trade-offs of a reverse proxy. (1) **Single point of failure** — if the proxy is down, the entire service is down. Mitigate by running multiple proxies behind DNS load balancing or a floating VIP (keepalived/VRRP). (2) **Latency** — the proxy adds a hop; in practice this is ~1 ms on a LAN, negligible, but in a chain of proxies (CDN -> WAF -> ALB -> service mesh sidecar) it adds up. (3) **Configuration complexity** — NGINX and Envoy configs can become massive; tooling like Istio's CRDs or HAProxy's templated configs help but introduce their own learning curve. (4) **Observability challenge** — when a request fails, you need to know if it failed at the client, the proxy, or the backend; the proxy must propagate trace headers and log enough to localize failures. (5) **Resource overhead** — Envoy sidecars in service meshes add ~50 MB RAM and ~5% CPU per pod, which at 10,000 pods is real money. The reverse proxy connects to many other system design concepts: it is the substrate of load balancing (Phase 5), the place where TLS termination happens (Phase 2 Topic 5), the foundation of service meshes (Phase 9), the implementation of API gateways (Phase 8), and the chokepoint for observability (Phase 12). Understanding reverse proxies deeply is essential because every production HTTP service has at least one, often a chain of three or four.

A client opens a TLS connection to `api.example.com:443`, which resolves to the reverse proxy's IP. The proxy terminates TLS (validates the cert, completes the handshake, decrypts incoming records) and parses the resulting HTTP request. 2. The proxy applies its middleware pipeline: rate limit check (is this client IP over quota?), authentication (is the JWT valid?), cache check (is this URL cached?), routing (which backend pool handles this path?). If the cache hits, the proxy returns the cached response without touching the backend. 3. The proxy picks a healthy backend from the pool using the configured algorithm (round-robin, least-connections, weighted). It polls each backend's `/health` endpoint every 5 seconds; backends that fail are removed from the pool automatically. The proxy forwards the request to the chosen backend over plaintext HTTP on port 8080 (inside the VPC), reads the response, and returns it to the client — possibly caching it for future requests.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Round-robin among healthy backends.
- Forward request to a backend.
- Start a tiny backend that returns its name in the body.
- Reverse proxy using http.server that round-robins across 3 backends
- With active health checks. Educational, single-process.
- Fast-fail: mark unhealthy after 2 consecutive failures so the
- Demo shows pool eviction within seconds (real systems use 3).
- Try at most len(healthy) picks to find a healthy one

**Defines:** `Backend`, `ReverseProxy`, `ProxyHandler`, `start_backend()`, `run_demo()`

```python
# Reverse proxy using http.server that round-robins across 3 backends
# with active health checks. Educational, single-process.

import http.server
import socketserver
import threading
import time
import urllib.request
import urllib.error
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Optional

@dataclass
class Backend:
    host: str
    port: int
    healthy: bool = True
    last_check: float = 0.0
    consecutive_failures: int = 0

    @property
    def url(self) -> str:
        return f"http://{self.host}:{self.port}"

    def check_health(self, path: str = "/health") -> bool:
        try:
            req = urllib.request.Request(f"{self.url}{path}", method="GET")
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=1.0) as resp:
                ok = resp.status == 200
        except Exception:
            ok = False
        self.last_check = time.time()
        if ok:
            self.consecutive_failures = 0
            self.healthy = True
        else:
            self.consecutive_failures += 1
            # Fast-fail: mark unhealthy after 2 consecutive failures so the
            # demo shows pool eviction within seconds (real systems use 3).
            if self.consecutive_failures >= 2:
                self.healthy = False
        return self.healthy

@dataclass
class ReverseProxy:
    backends: list
    rr_index: int = 0
    lock: threading.Lock = field(default_factory=threading.Lock)
    stats: dict = field(default_factory=lambda: {
        "requests": 0, "backend_2xx": 0, "backend_4xx": 0,
        "backend_5xx": 0, "backend_errors": 0, "no_healthy": 0,
    })

    def pick_backend(self) -> Optional[Backend]:
        """Round-robin among healthy backends."""
        with self.lock:
            healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
            if not healthy:
                return None
            # Try at most len(healthy) picks to find a healthy one
            for _ in range(len(self.backends)):
                b = self.backends[self.rr_index % len(self.backends)]
                self.rr_index += 1
                if b.healthy:
                    return b
            return None

    def forward(self, method: str, path: str, headers: dict,
                body: bytes) -> tuple:
        """Forward request to a backend. Returns (status, body, backend_url)."""
        backend = self.pick_backend()
        self.stats["requests"] += 1
        if backend is None:
            self.stats["no_healthy"] += 1
            return (503, b"no healthy backends\n", "-")

        url = f"{backend.url}{path}"
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, data=body if body else None,
                                     method=method)
        for k, v in headers.items():
            if k.lower() in ("host", "content-length", "connection"):
                continue
            req.add_header(k, v)
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=2.0) as resp:
                status = resp.status
                resp_body = resp.read()
                if 200 <= status < 300:
                    self.stats["backend_2xx"] += 1
                elif 400 <= status < 500:
                    self.stats["backend_4xx"] += 1
                else:
                    self.stats["backend_5xx"] += 1
                return (status, resp_body, backend.url)
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            self.stats["backend_4xx" if e.code < 500 else "backend_5xx"] += 1
            return (e.code, e.read(), backend.url)
        except Exception as e:
            self.stats["backend_errors"] += 1
            # Passive health check: mark the backend unhealthy immediately on
            # connection errors so the pool self-heals within a few requests
            # (real systems use 3 strikes to avoid flapping).
            backend.consecutive_failures += 1
            if backend.consecutive_failures >= 2:
                backend.healthy = False
            return (502, f"bad gateway: {e}\n".encode(), backend.url)

    def health_check_loop(self, stop_event: threading.Event,
                          interval: float = 5.0) -> None:
        while not stop_event.is_set():
            for b in self.backends:
                b.check_health()
            time.sleep(interval)

PROXY: Optional[ReverseProxy] = None

class ProxyHandler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def _handle(self):
        if PROXY is None:
            self.send_response(503)
            self.end_headers()
            return
        body = b""
        if self.command in ("POST", "PUT", "PATCH"):
            length = int(self.headers.get("Content-Length", 0))
            body = self.rfile.read(length) if length else b""
        status, resp_body, backend_url = PROXY.forward(
            self.command, self.path, dict(self.headers), body)
        self.send_response(status)
        self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("X-Served-By", backend_url)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(resp_body)))
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(resp_body)

    def do_GET(self):    self._handle()
    def do_POST(self):   self._handle()
    def do_PUT(self):    self._handle()
    def do_DELETE(self): self._handle()

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        # Custom log: include backend
        print(f"  [proxy] {self.command} {self.path} -> {args[1]}")

def start_backend(port: int, name: str, healthy: bool = True) -> threading.Thread:
    """Start a tiny backend that returns its name in the body."""
    class Handler(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def do_GET(self):
            if self.path == "/health":
                self.send_response(200 if healthy else 500)
                self.end_headers()
                self.wfile.write(b"ok" if healthy else b"down")
                return
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            body = f'{{"backend":"{name}","port":{port},"path":"{self.path}"}}'.encode()
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(body)
        def log_message(self, *a): pass
    server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), Handler)
    t = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
    t.start()
    t._server = server
    return t

def run_demo():
    print("=== Reverse Proxy Demo ===\n")
    # Start 3 backends on ports 9001, 9002, 9003
    backend_threads = []
    for port, name in [(9001, "backend-A"), (9002, "backend-B"),
                        (9003, "backend-C")]:
        t = start_backend(port, name)
        backend_threads.append(t)
        print(f"  started {name} on 127.0.0.1:{port}")

    backends = [
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9001),
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9002),
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9003),
    ]
    global PROXY
    PROXY = ReverseProxy(backends=backends)

    # Start health-check loop in background (2s interval so the demo
    # can observe pool eviction within a few seconds of failure).
    stop = threading.Event()
    hc = threading.Thread(target=PROXY.health_check_loop, args=(stop,),
                          kwargs={"interval": 2.0}, daemon=True)
    hc.start()

    # Start the proxy on port 9000
    proxy_server = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 9000),
                                                   ProxyHandler)
    proxy_thread = threading.Thread(target=proxy_server.serve_forever,
                                    daemon=True)
    proxy_thread.start()
    print(f"  started reverse proxy on 127.0.0.1:9000\n")

    # Send 6 requests through the proxy and observe round-robin distribution
    print("--- Sending 6 requests through the proxy (expect round-robin) ---")
    for i in range(6):
        req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/users")
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
                body = resp.read().decode()
                served_by = resp.headers.get("X-Served-By", "?")
                print(f"  req {i+1}: status={resp.status} "
                      f"served_by={served_by} body={body}")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            print(f"  req {i+1}: status={e.code} (expected: backend failure)")

    # Simulate backend B going down: stop its server
    print("\n--- Simulating backend-B failure (shutting it down) ---")
    backend_threads[1]._server.shutdown()
    # Wait long enough for active health check (2s interval) + buffer.
    time.sleep(3.0)
    print(f"  backend-B healthy flag: {backends[1].healthy} "
          f"(expected False after 2 consecutive health check failures)")
    print(f"  note: passive check via connection errors also marks unhealthy "
          f"after 2 strikes; this demo shows both working together")

    # Send 6 more requests — should observe some 502s on the first hit to B
    # (passive check kicks in), then only A and C going forward.
    print("\n--- Sending 6 more requests (B is unhealthy; A and C only) ---")
    for i in range(6):
        req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:9000/api/users")
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req) as resp:
                served_by = resp.headers.get("X-Served-By", "?")
                body = resp.read().decode()
                print(f"  req {i+7}: status={resp.status} "
                      f"served_by={served_by} body={body}")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            served_by = e.headers.get("X-Served-By", "?") if e.headers else "?"
            print(f"  req {i+7}: status={e.code} served_by={served_by} "
                  f"(passive check kicking in: marking B unhealthy)")

    print(f"\n--- Final stats ---\n  {PROXY.stats}")
    stop.set()
    proxy_server.shutdown()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_demo()
```
